Rulings of Ramadan: who pays fidyah, sunnahs of fasting, timing mistakes, taraweeh, zakat al-fitr and Eid prayer, with his preferred positions. Temporary illness, travel and exhaustion require only make-up. Eating after fajr by mistake leaves the fast valid; breaking early does not. He dwells on the two reasons named for punishment: not believing in Allah and not urging the feeding of the poor. Tazkiyah Pearls 6: The Soul, the Cycle and the Qalb (Subconscious)

How the nafs works and is tamed, the conscience, the thought-action-feeling cycle, and changing feelings by changing what enters the heart. He deepens the picture of the nafs: made from the earth, it is programmed for survival and superiority, indifferent to whether means are lawful, unaware of what is truly good for you, unwilling to act unless there is something in it for itself, and unable to accept delayed reward, much like a selfish toddler. Many of its convictions, such as believing you deserve good things, should be kept but rewired to the right source; those whose nafs lost that belief through abuse need therapy. The goal is to tame the nafs, not break it, and he describes five levels for each behaviour, from total surrender to the nafs through a seesaw, forced compliance and resigned habit, to agreement. The conscience is the ruh's influence on the nafs, and its death is the beginning of death. He then presents the cycle in which thoughts, actions and feelings shape one another: we control our actions fully, our thoughts partly through reflection, and our feelings not at all. A Damascene story of a woman who set out to poison her mother-in-law with nightly massages shows good actions changing hatred into love. Feelings come from the heart's mixing pot of what we see, hear, think and are surrounded by, so he asks listeners to change their inputs and expectations patiently, since tazkiyah is slow. Tazkiyah: purifying and training the self Behaviour change: the thought-action-feeling cycle and habits Selfishness, greed of the soul (shuhh) and selflessness Mental health, anxiety and emotional wellbeing Character and manners (akhlaq) Salah: its meaning, etiquette and significance The nafs is programmed for survival. Coming from the soil of the earth, the nafs, like all life, wants to survive, dominate and take in the most energy for the least effort. It cares about outcomes, not means. Halal or haram means nothing to it; it loves you but does not know what is best, which is why domesticated animals and people overeat. There must be something in it for the nafs. Selflessness is hard because the nafs resists anything that profits it nothing, such as strengthening someone else; it is not evil, just programmed, so we do not hate it. No delayed reward: a toddler inside. A bird in the hand beats ten in the tree; the nafs trusts no one and is a selfish child we carry within. Keep its convictions, change the reasons. Believing you deserve good things is essential and should be rewired to Allah as its source; those whose nafs lost it through abuse need real therapy. Tame the nafs, do not break it. A broken nafs leaves a person without integrity or courage; taming happens in levels. Level one: no resistance. Like a parent who gives a two-year-old everything, the person simply submits to whatever the nafs wants. Level two: the seesaw. Some days you win and some days the nafs wins; your level differs for each behaviour. Level three: forcing the nafs. The nafs hates it but has no choice, as with most people going to work or sometimes to Fajr. Level four: the nafs gives up. It stops fighting and the act becomes habit, though without passion and with the nafs still thinking it wasteful. Level five: the nafs agrees. As in play, the nafs wants what you want; the hope is to reach this for the deeds that bring us close to Allah. The conscience: the ruh's effect on the nafs. The stronger the spirit's influence on the nafs, the stronger the conscience; it is one nafs with different states. The death of the conscience. Death begins when the spirit no longer influences the nafs; a good upbringing, environment and values of compassion strengthen the spirit. Connection to Allah as an endless source. Those good before Islam became good in Islam; without a link to Allah the spirit shrivels and needs constant upkeep. The cycle of thoughts, actions and feelings. Each one affects and is affected by the other two, so the cycle is always virtuous or vicious. How much of each we control. We control all our actions, a variable share of our thoughts that grows with contemplation, and none of our feelings directly. Breaking a vicious cycle. Disliking someone breeds negative thoughts and bad actions that deepen the dislike; jam a rod in the wheel by deliberately thinking and acting well. The mother-in-law and the poison lotion. A Damascene apothecary gave a woman plain lotion to massage her mother-in-law nightly; after twenty days she came back begging for an antidote because she now loved her. Feelings are the strongest part of the cycle. Strong feelings power both thoughts and actions, raising the question of how to influence what we cannot control. The qalb's four inputs. The heart mixes what we see, what we hear, our environment and our thoughts, and its output is our emotions. The heart loves what it is fed, with a lag. Feeding it haram sights, sounds, company and thoughts makes it love haram; changes take months to show as old input filters out. Turning a hated chore neutral through expectations. Taking out garbage or driving siblings feels awful when thought of negatively; treating it as a given makes the heart neutral about it. Learning to enjoy what is not play, including salah. Changing outlook and associations can make a non-playful act joyful, which is how prayer moves from habit to enjoyment. Tazkiyah is slow, not an aha moment. Few are granted a sudden transformation; most must identify their nafs and change thoughts and inputs to change behaviour over time. Why everyone wants a front lawn. Our subconscious absorbed the background of films, so we want houses, cars and lawns without knowing why; change what you look at, listen to and surround yourself with. Everything returns to this cycle. These simple principles let you take back control, changing how you feel about even tiring acts of worship. A ten-point plan for Ramadan: intention, fasting with excellence, Quran, dhikr, prayer, knowledge, relationships, service, dua, and planning your life. Respecting an opportunity means planning for it, and Ramadan never arrives by surprise. Second, fast with excellence: fasting is not a handicap but proof of how little you need, a step further from the forbidden, and a training of the self that should extend to the tongue, eyes, ears and hands. Third, enjoy the Quran through a daily portion that is never skipped and a few verses kept for reflection, since Ramadan is the annual Quran retreat. Fourth, build daily dhikr in place of irritation, chatter and scrolling. Fifth, invest in prayer, with the young standing the full taraweeh. Envy and anger as the two toxic results of self-value swinging low, with their Quranic examples and practical cures. Continuing his image of self-value as a pendulum, he examines what happens when it swings toward inferiority. Envy is discomfort at someone else having something, not a wish to have it yourself; healthy aspiration is a different thing and the Prophet allowed it only for knowledge and generous wealth. Envy comes from attaching value to things and seeing others as threats. He ranks three kinds: envy over worldly goods, envy over worldly gains reached through religious work, and the subtlest, envy over someone's closeness to Allah, which is what drove Qabil. Both Quranic envy stories, Qabil and Habil and Yusuf's brothers, involve siblings and murder, and he corrects the popular marriage explanation of the first. The cure is a jama'ah mindset: seeing everyone as teammates so their success is your win, asking yourself repeatedly why you felt discomfort, and becoming the person people want to share good news with, while being careful not to provoke envy in others. Anger arises when self-value is threatened; every emotion born of fluctuating self-value is toxic, unlike anger for Allah's sake at oppression. Whoever can trigger you holds your remote control. Through children who sense ego-driven anger and a road-rage example, he shows that envy and anger are about us, and asks people to find their triggers and respond calmly. In 49:12 he explains why eating a dead brother's flesh fits backbiting on three counts: the absent cannot defend themselves, something is taken from them, and the gain is a disgusting boost to one's own ego. The great intercession: after years of waiting humanity goes from Adam to Isa, each declines, and the Prophet prostrates beneath the Throne until judgment begins. Tawakkul as the bridge between belief and action: full effort, dependence on Allah and contentment with His decree, and the freedom it brings. He first explains why the series builds foundations like self-worth, compassion and mortality before any talk of spiritual states: emotional reminders without clear fundamentals give a short-lived high. Tawakkul links theology to practice, and it rests on the fact that we do not know what is best for us, as the Quran says and as a folk tale about a farmer's shifting fortunes shows. Nothing arrives labelled as blessing or punishment; we label it by how we respond, and no one can declare a hardship to be Allah's wrath. Hardships met with patience are tax-free, while blessings carry a debt of gratitude. After separating what you can control from what you cannot, he defines three components: doing your genuine best, without which tawakkul becomes a numbing excuse for passivity; depending on Allah for the outcome, since there are endless ways to fail even when prepared; and contentment with His decree, never with your own effort, expressed as gratitude in ease and perseverance in hardship. A great scholar who smiled on hearing of his son's death illustrates that contentment. The benefits are freedom from relying on your deeds, from resentment against Allah, the union of ambition and acceptance, courage to do what is right, and never feeling forgotten. Finally, of the four possible pairings of effort and outcome, the person of tawakkul sees good as Allah's gift and bad as a cause for self-review. The central verse of al-Ahzab says a believer does not treat Allah's decree as optional; commands are never harmful, and what feels hard is our own selfishness. The trust refused by the heavens, earth and mountains is freedom of choice, which only humans have, which is why reward and punishment exist; he urges parents to let children face the consequences of their choices. From Saba he argues that communities survive through healthy dialogue, and that the Quran's 'either we or you are guided' expresses a creed that follows evidence and accepts nothing blindly, since only certainty holds in hardship. The one piece of advice in Saba is to dedicate oneself to Allah and reflect deeply, because behaviour follows inner conviction, as the Prophet's contemplation at Hira shows. Fatir links reverence to understanding creation, so Muslims should never shy away from science. He closes by urging full effort in the last ten nights. Obedience is what Allah requires of us, but it is more profound than it seems, and each surah unpacks it from a different angle. Al-Ahzab: obeying when it is hardest. Obeying Allah when there are many reasons not to is the way out of every difficulty and from darkness to light. Saba: how a community obeys. Communal obedience looks different from individual obedience and has its own measures; few surahs address it. Fatir: obedience through knowledge. Allah cannot be obeyed through ignorance; dignity comes from obeying Him the way He wants, not the way we want. Ya-Sin: life is more than breathing. Opening the second Quranic Themes series with stewardship (khilafah), read through Adam, the Children of Israel and Ibrahim in Al-Baqarah. He opens the year's series by explaining that the Quran returns to themes rather than repeating itself, because a concept only lands when it is approached several times in different ways. The first theme is stewardship: the human being is a khalifa, not in a political sense but as someone left responsible for things on another's behalf, who will be asked how he cared for them. He reads three passages of Al-Baqarah as three kinds of steward. Adam failed his first test because he did not yet understand his own nafs and disliked being responsible, mortal and a servant; he repented with the words Allah gave him and never knowingly disobeyed again, and we are handed his lesson without paying his price. The Children of Israel are the example of failure: after clear signs they took the calf, said they hear and disobey, and their hearts were soaked in that love until it could not be removed; and they became greedy for mere life, a fear of death that makes a person sell out every principle. Ibrahim is the steward who passed test after test and was made an imam. He asks listeners to take responsibility seriously, use Ramadan to wash out sins that have settled in the heart, and rank values above survival. A steward is responsible for something on someone else's behalf; the human being is a khalifa spiritually, not politically, and worships Allah through that responsibility and will be asked about it. Adam placed on earth as a khalifa. Adam begins like any of us, enjoying breath, food and companionship without yet knowing why, and is told he will be a steward on earth. Three truths the nafs dislikes. Adam was uncomfortable being responsible, being mortal and being a servant, the same three things people resist today. Sent down: shame and loss. On earth Adam lost safety, plenty and companionship, but what hurt most was the shame of having disobeyed Allah. Words of repentance given to Adam. Not yet knowing what tawbah was, Adam was taught words to say, admitting he had wronged himself, and Allah accepted his repentance. A scripted lesson, not a return to Paradise. Adam was still sent down because earth was his purpose; the episode teaches obedience, restraining the nafs and owning responsibility for oneself and one's family. Follow the guidance; Adam never knowingly sinned again. Whoever follows Allah's guidance has nothing to fear; we receive the solved example for free, and Adam's later mistakes were only forgetfulness and lack of knowledge. Taking the calf after clear signs. Stewardship is both obligation and opportunity; Allah teaches it through good and failed examples, starting with a people who worshipped the calf after Musa's miracles. The covenant under the raised mountain. Their covenant was renewed under the mountain; the Torah taught the same responsibility the Quran teaches, to shepherd the wellbeing of those around you. Hearts soaked in the love of the calf. The word for 'made to drink' means soaked through; sin becomes deadly when it stays in the heart until it cannot be separated, like cloth left in perfume or sewage. Ramadan can rid the heart of a soaked sin. A sin that persists despite knowing it is haram has been absorbed by the heart; Ramadan is a rare chance to remove it, and stewardship is impossible without doing so. Greed for mere life. Being the most eager for life means a crippling fear of death; such a person will compromise any principle and cannot even trust himself to protect his own family. A steward's priorities are values, in the right order. Muslims need to know not only Islam's values and ethics but how they rank, otherwise they discard a value that should never be dropped. Our heroes stood their ground under threat. Prolonging life is not a value in itself; the people we honour held to their principles with a gun to their heads, which is what stewardship and manhood mean. Three kinds of steward. Adam erred then got it right, the Children of Israel kept failing by choice, and Ibrahim got it right without the initial mistake. Ibrahim tested with trial after trial. Ibrahim spoke against his people's idols, was thrown into the fire, expelled, debated star worshippers and a king, and passed every test. Made an imam for mankind. Allah made him a leader; he died with few followers yet is now honoured by most of humanity, and he then asked about his descendants. See yourself as a steward who will be asked how you cared for yourself, your family and your community. Use Ramadan to uproot a sin that has settled in your heart before it becomes permanent. Use Ramadan to call on Allah directly; He is near and responds. Read the Quran yourself so you own your narrative, including on combat. Why As-Saffat tells the stories of Ilyas, Lut and Yunus briefly: each demands accepting the unseen and judgements whose wisdom is hidden. He restates the surah's axis: submission to Allah both in matters wholly unseen and in commands whose wisdom we cannot grasp, and shows how the stories of Nuh, Ibrahim and Musa fit it. Ilyas is a prophet the Arabs never knew and the Quran barely describes; the Torah's account may be heard but neither believed nor denied, so accepting him as Allah presents him is itself faith in the unseen. Along the way he explains the grammar of 'the best of creators', the difference between a messenger with a law and a prophet, and why 'seal of the prophets' closes both. Lut's story is told without the closing praise given to other prophets because his name has been dragged into the sin of his people. He argues that the prohibition stands whether or not its full wisdom is understood, then speaks frankly: desire is innate but its direction is shaped by upbringing, culture, abuse and other factors; the sin is the act, not the feeling; oversimplifying the issue has cost Muslims the argument. Disapproval never permits injustice toward anyone. Finally, Yunus's people were spared while Lut's were destroyed, and no one can claim to know why. He asks for submission, careful understanding and fairness. Obedience to Allah and the Messenger Eman: faith, certainty, doubt Methodology: how to read texts, tafsir method, intellectual approach Gender relations, chastity and modesty Justice and refusing oppression Stories of earlier prophets Muslim identity and life in the West / Canada Education, schools and learning disorders Every surah has its own axis. Recap: the stories in a surah serve the purpose for which it was revealed, and each surah of this group looks at obedience differently. Two kinds of hidden: unseen realities and unseen wisdom. Some things, like angels, are known only through revelation; some commands have reasons we cannot reach. As-Saffat addresses obedience in both. Recap: Nuh's ship and Ibrahim's sacrifice. Both were commanded to do what made no visible sense and obeyed. Why Musa's story is compressed here. Elsewhere each surah picks a distinctive part of Musa's story; here it is summarised because all of it fits the axis. Musa's life as a chain of puzzling commands. Cast into the river, raised in Pharaoh's palace, sent to Madyan, called at the fire, sent to the sea, told to enter the gate: each time he obeyed without knowing the end. Ilyas: a prophet we barely know, and the idol Baal. After reciting the passage he notes that Ilyas appears only here with a story; Baal was a Canaanite deity of strength, likely linked to Baalbek. "The best of creators" and the grammar of substitution. The superlative glorifies Allah without implying rival creators; Allah, your Lord and Lord of your forefathers are appositives sharing the same case, with another reading parsing it differently. The Torah's account of Ilyas and Al-Yasa'. A king married a Canaanite princess, idol worship spread, the queen threatened Ilyas, and in that account he was raised up and prophethood passed to Al-Yasa'. Rejection, the sincere servants, and peace upon Il-Yasin. His people denied him and will be brought to account; the greeting is extended to his followers, and we accept the wording without knowing why. How to treat reports from the People of the Book. They may be narrated but neither believed nor denied; anything contradicting the Quran is rejected, and prior law is used in rulings only when nothing else exists. Messengers whose stories we were not told. The Prophet spoke at length about many prophets but said nothing about Ilyas; some messengers are simply unknown to us. Mursal, rasul and nabi; the seal of the prophets. A rasul brings a new law, a nabi follows an earlier one; because Muhammad is the seal of the prophets, neither prophet nor messenger comes after him. Which prophets followed earlier laws. Lut followed Ibrahim's law, Ilyas, Yunus, Zakariyya and Yahya followed Musa's, while Isa brought a law that lifted some prohibitions. The purpose of Ilyas's story: accepting what we do not know. The surah names a prophet and gives almost no detail, teaching acceptance of the unseen as part of faith. Lut was sent to a people whose conduct went against sound nature, something a man in ordinary circumstances would find repugnant. Forbidden even when the full reason is not clear. Harms of zina are obvious, the wisdom here may be harder to spell out, but what Allah forbids is forbidden; the pork-worm argument shows how weak invented reasons can be. Unlike the other prophets, Lut is not followed by the line of praise among later generations, because his name is still attacked; with Allah he is among the greatest. Against the Arabian custom that warriors take all spoils, Allah directs it to the Prophet, his kin, orphans, the needy and the stranded traveller, whom he likens to a refugee. A practical walk through the rulings of Ramadan fasting: intention, what breaks and does not break the fast, exemptions, expiations, sunnahs, tarawih, zakat al-fitr and Eid. In his yearly fiqh of Ramadan class he gives the majority positions of the four schools rather than one madhab, noting that the schools evolve and that a follower may take the local imam's madhab for Ramadan. He starts with intention: the Ramadan fast needs an intention before dawn, and waking for suhoor is enough, though he finds the Maliki view of one intention for the whole month reasonable. His general rule is that anything taken in intentionally that counts medically as nourishment breaks the fast. He lists the six agreed invalidators, the things that do not break the fast, and the disputed cases such as inhalers, drops, IV lines and suppositories, giving his own view and repeating that health comes before ritual. He covers who may break the fast (the ill, travellers, pregnant and nursing women, the severely fatigued), the duty to make up days before the next Ramadan, and when children should begin fasting. He explains the major and minor expiations with current dollar amounts and who owes them, including the terminally ill and the elderly, and the manners expected of those who cannot fast. He closes with the sunnahs of suhoor and iftar, fasting from sin, staying through tarawih, zakat al-fitr and holding one Eid prayer per community. Children should learn the rulings early and adults need them to explain Ramadan and help the ill and elderly. He gives majority positions across the four schools, notes that schools evolve over time, and says a madhab follower may adopt the local imam's madhab for Ramadan. The intention for the Ramadan fast. A voluntary fast can be intended mid-morning, but Ramadan and make-up fasts need an intention before dawn; it need not be spoken and waking for suhoor counts. He favours the Maliki view that one intention covers the whole month. The general rule: intentional nourishment breaks the fast. Anything taken into the body intentionally that meets the medical definition of nourishment invalidates the fast; knowing this spares people panic over every small question. Invalidator: eating and drinking on purpose. Breaking a Ramadan day deliberately, often out of anger or a fit of temper, is a major sin; the day is made up and repentance accepted, but the reward of that obligatory day can never be regained. Invalidator: intercourse or its equivalent. Relations between spouses during the day, or deliberately reaching orgasm, break the fast and carry a heavy expiation. Invalidator: deliberate vomiting. Making oneself vomit breaks the fast; someone who feels sick should first intend to break the fast under the illness exemption and then vomit. He offers help to anyone struggling with bulimia. Invalidator: parenteral nourishment. Nourishment by IV, under the skin or into the muscle breaks the fast; in hospital, ask whether what you were given was nourishment. Vitamins do not count. Invalidator: smoking and vaping. Any form of smoking, including shisha and vaping, breaks the fast. Invalidator: menstruation or childbirth. If bleeding begins even a moment before maghrib, that day is lost and must be repeated. He recaps the six agreed invalidators. Does not break: brushing teeth and miswak. Brushing or using miswak is fine as long as toothpaste is not swallowed. Does not break: eating or drinking forgetfully. Allah simply fed the forgetful person. If you see someone eating forgetfully, let them finish rather than reminding them mid-swallow and ruining their fast, unless they are plainly not fasting. Does not break: a wet dream. A wet dream during a daytime nap does not affect the fast, and one at night only requires ghusl before praying. Does not break: non-nourishing injections; caution for diabetics. B12, antibiotics, insulin, flu shots and vaccines given into muscle or under the skin are fine. Diabetics must ask their physician weeks before Ramadan whether they can fast; as a resident he saw elderly patients return repeatedly with dangerous sugar levels. Does not break: swallowing one's own saliva. Swallowing saliva does not break the fast, even if deliberately collected, though doing so is distasteful. Does not break: water left after wudu. Rinsing the mouth vigorously is disliked while fasting, but there is no need to be obsessive; whatever drops remain after a normal wudu are forgiven. Fasting rests on knowing what you are doing and why. Disputed: inhalers. Scholars differ; he sees no problem with using an inhaler as needed for asthma, COPD or other lung disease. Disputed: eye and ear drops. He holds that medical drops do not break the fast, treating a stray drop like the water left after wudu, since none of it is nourishment. Disputed: non-nourishing IV infusions. Unpacking the two-word prophetic command saddidu wa qaribu: approach with balance and hit the objective. Al-Insan calls through reward and Al-Mursalat through warning: dawah needs both wings, and actions, not words, show belief. After a surah that addresses the intellect, he presents Al-Insan and Al-Mursalat as two other valid ways of calling to Allah: hope of reward and warning of punishment. Each emphasises one but includes the other, because dawah is a bird with two wings. A story from his village shows that different people need different keys: farmers unmoved by talk of Paradise were stirred by a talk on Hell. Al-Insan begins by reminding us we were once nothing, so life itself is the first gift, then shows two paths, the righteous who feed others for Allah's sake wanting no thanks, and a lavish Paradise in which Allah graciously tells people they earned it. The way there is dhikr morning and evening and night prayer; we are destined for Paradise, but fulfilling that destiny is our choice. Al-Mursalat swears by winds that bring either blessing or harm: nothing comes labelled, we decide what a reminder becomes. Three points for keeping marriages: build on ihsan rather than rights, never tolerate abuse, and handle inevitable disputes wisely while protecting the children. In the last of three khutbahs on marriage, he says keeping marriages intact used to come naturally but is now failing. His first point is that Islamic marriage rests on ihsan: the obligations are few, a husband provides and protects and a wife stays loyal and cares for the children, so everything else is an act of love. When we treat extras as rights, any shortfall breeds resentment; when we see them as gifts, we feel grateful and give back. Men need respect and someone who stands by them in hard times, which he draws from the Prophet's lifelong love for Khadijah, who believed in him when others rejected him; women, he thinks, need to feel needed, loved and noticed. Second, abuse of any kind is never acceptable, though the term should be defined carefully, and the community must protect the abused and rehabilitate the abuser internally. Third, disputes are guaranteed even in the Prophet's household, so seek help from unbiased people who will tell you that you are wrong, not parents who inflame things. Divorce is sometimes right, as with Zayd and Zaynab, but children must never be weaponized. He closes by urging the community to invest its resources in helping people marry and stay married. Marriage and the relationship between spouses Ihsan and excellence in worship Marriage and the relationship between spouses The Prophet's attributes, character and example The unlawfulness of harm and protecting others Marriage and the relationship between spouses Parenting and raising children Family: parents, relatives, kinship ties Keeping marriages is now the challenge. Third and final marriage khutbah; earlier generations stayed married for 30 to 50 years without imams addressing it, but marriages are now failing even once they begin. Point one: marriage is built on ihsan. The obligations are few: the husband protects and provides food, clothing and a home; the wife stays loyal and cares for the children. Obligation breeds no gratitude, extras do. Our parents' habits make the list seem longer; what is owed draws no thanks and its absence causes anger, while what is extra is received with appreciation, in both directions. The reward of excellence is excellence. Extras answered with extras fill a marriage with the love and mercy Allah described; entitlement fills it with resentment, and what was extra to begin with should not upset you when missing. His later marriages were strategic: uniting tribes and the house of Abraham and giving eminent women autonomy at a hard time. Aisha's jealousy of Khadijah. He loved Khadijah until he died; Aisha was jealous only of her, though she had died years earlier, and he sent portions of every gift to Khadijah's friends. Khadijah's friends while an army waited. He halted an army and sat half an hour under a tree with three elderly women, reminiscing about Khadijah. He knew her footsteps. Years after her death he sat up at footsteps that sounded like hers; told to remarry, he asked who could take her place. She stood by me when others turned away. When Aisha said he had better, he answered that Khadijah believed in him and supported him when people rejected him; loyalty in hardship is what men remember. What women need, and respect above love. From observation he thinks women want to feel needed, loved and attended to; for men respect matters even more than love, and weakening your husband makes no sense. Even the best had marital quarrels. The Prophet found Ali sleeping on the masjid dust after a quarrel and sent him home; difficulties are part of life, but answer them with excellence and love. Point two: abuse is never acceptable. Physical, verbal, financial or social abuse is never allowed, but the term, especially emotional abuse, must be defined carefully; it happens in both directions and the abused must be protected. The Prophet never struck anyone. Good people with bad tempers still abuse, and society must protect the other party; nothing in Islam permits abuse, and the Prophet never raised his hand except in combat. Deal with abuse within the community. Outsiders handling our cases do not share our values; families and friends must not look away, the abused must be protected and the abuser educated and treated. 'The wrapped one' names the Prophet's humanity, and he reminds the audience that everyone remains a frightened child inside who must hold on to Allah. Turning to the verses, he explains qum as taking on a responsibility, not merely standing; the night prayer means the waking part of the night, illustrated by biphasic sleep, napping, and a critique of the nine-to-five. The point is that you need this prayer. The two surahs are named after this image: one layer you build for yourself, one that people see. If either drops, the dawah will not work, and both surahs point back to one crucial moment. Names that return the Prophet to moment zero. Every other prophet is called by his first name in the Quran, but the Prophet only by titles. In the depths of his ordeal he still gave da'wah, first crediting Allah for his knowledge, then calling his fellow prisoners to the One, the Subduer. After urging listeners to learn and memorize the final quarter of the Quran a few verses at a time, he returns to verses 22 and 23. He clears away the old arguments about decree: a god who did not know the future would not deserve worship, knowing is not causing, time does not apply to Allah, and anyone sitting in the room can see they have real choices. The verse concerns what lies outside our control, like a never-smoking marathon runner's terminal cancer, and its stated purpose is practical: not to over-grieve losses with endless 'if onlys', nor to become entitled and vain over success that Allah often bailed us out to achieve. He describes an inner two-layer pendulum, confidence against vanity or worthlessness and humility against arrogance or inferiority, which life's bumps swing unless held in the middle by remembering that all was written. Vanity and arrogance produce self-centredness, which the verse calls stinginess, and a culture that encourages it; material events cause spiritual swings that return as material behaviour. Allah is the Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy, needing none of it. Verse 25 explains the surah's name: prophets were sent with the Book, the Balance and iron, so faith must be joined to strength and use of the world, a balance the Prophet embodied. A saved believer recalls the companion who nearly ruined him by asking 'do you really believe?'; the tree of Zaqqum; and the blind rush in forefathers' footsteps. He restates the surah's theme: belief in the unseen is not switching off the mind, since the first command was 'read', meaning observe and analyse; once reason brings you to Allah, you accept what He tells and decrees even when its wisdom is hidden. In Paradise one of the saved recalls a companion, perhaps a friend, perhaps his own self or a jinn, who asked whether he truly believed he would be raised and judged. That question, he says, is answered with a way of life, not a word: belief in the reckoning should visibly change how one speaks, earns, looks and treats people, and trying to keep a foot in both camps is the compromise the Quran condemns. The saved man looks down, sees his companion in the depths of Hell, and credits his escape to Allah's favour alone, a moment worth working for. He reads 'we will not die except our first death' as the saved man quoting his old companion's taunt. Zaqqum is a trial: those who mock its description, like those who mocked the nineteen angels, are tested by it. Finally the doomed rushed after their forefathers without thinking, a blind following Islam rejects for Muslims too, and he separates accepting the unseen from believing superstition. Surat Saba' Summary

Surat Saba' read as a guide to how whole societies submit to Allah: eight factors that keep civilizations standing and the arrogance that topples them. He places Saba' in the cluster from Al-Ahzab to Az-Zumar on submission to Allah. Al-Ahzab addressed individuals obeying in hardship; Saba' addresses societies. Societies that submit keep their civilizations; those deluded by superiority fall. He draws out a series of factors. First, knowledge joined with mercy, noting that the opening page pairs Allah's knowledge with Al-Rahim placed before Al-Ghafur. Second, gratitude, shown in Dawud and Sulayman, whose strength even commanded the jinn people now fear superstitiously; the jinn's false claim to know the unseen was exposed when Sulayman died leaning on his staff. Gratitude means passing blessings on to those in need. Third, humility: the people of Saba' had two gardens, turned from gratitude, sought to dominate trade routes, and were scattered after the dam burst. Fourth, certainty: Iblis gains power only through doubt, so societies must not treat Allah's law like human legislation. Fifth, respectful dialogue: the 'Say' verses begin and end with belief, refuse to presume who is guided, attribute crime to ourselves and let results judge. Sixth, no blind following: followers remain accountable and must hold leaders to account. Seventh, wealth is distributed unevenly so people care for one another, hence zakat. Eighth, collective reflection to solve a society's problems. Community building, cooperation and the ummah Islamic history and civilization Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation Humility vs vanity and arrogance Eman: faith, certainty, doubt Tolerance, pluralism and dealing with difference Leadership, governance and institutions Wealth, asceticism (zuhd), consumerism and money Conspiracy thinking and critical thinking Saba': submission seen from the level of society. Individuals know how to obey through prayer and fasting; Saba' explains how whole societies obey, and why civilizations that do so endure while arrogant ones fall. Knowledge together with mercy. The opening verses join Allah's encompassing knowledge with mercy; a society needs both to keep flourishing. Dawud and Sulayman: gratitude and the jinn exposed. Allah's favours to Dawud and Sulayman, the command to work in gratitude, and the jinn who kept toiling unaware that Sulayman had died. The cluster from Al-Ahzab to Az-Zumar on submission. Allah gave us free will and asks us to surrender it to His; Al-Ahzab dealt with individuals obeying in hard circumstances, Saba' deals with societies. First factor: knowledge and mercy. Only here does Al-Rahim precede Al-Ghafur, paired with Allah's knowledge; the page closes with those given knowledge recognising the truth. Second factor: gratitude in the kingdom of Dawud and Sulayman. They built strong societies and even commanded the jinn, whom people today fear through superstition; when gratitude stops, Allah's good stops. Sulayman's death and the jinn's illusion of knowing the unseen. Termites ate his staff before the jinn realised he had died, exposing their false claim; a society shows gratitude by passing its blessings to those in need. The people of Saba': two gardens and ingratitude. Saba' was told to eat and give thanks but turned away and asked Allah to lengthen the distance between their journeys, so they were scattered. Third factor: humility; arrogance brought the dam down. Saba' wanted to disrupt the safe route between Yemen and Syria so traders would need their protection; the dam of Marib burst and they migrated. Societies must not see themselves as superior to other peoples. Fourth factor: certainty against Iblis's doubt. Iblis's assumption about humans proved true for many, yet his only power is doubt; societies must hold Allah's law with certainty and not equate it with human laws. The 'Say' verses: how to argue with others. He walks through the series of commands to say, which set out how to debate those who differ from us. Fifth factor: the etiquette of dialogue. Begin and end with belief; say either we or you are guided rather than claiming victory; call our own deeds crimes and theirs mere deeds; and let results judge rather than endless theory. Sixth factor: no blind following. On Judgment Day the weak blame the arrogant leaders, who answer that they never forced them; following someone blindly does not excuse the follower. Holding leaders to account. Obeying leadership matters, but civilizations rise when followers question and scrutinise their leaders, something badly missing in our countries and communities. Seventh factor: wealth and its distribution. Wealth and children do not bring people near to Allah; He spreads and restricts provision so people care for one another, and whatever is spent He replaces. Hence zakat and Abu Bakr's stand against those who withheld it. Eighth factor: stand for Allah and reflect. Allah asks people to stand in pairs and alone and think, and they will conclude the Prophet brought guidance; societies must reflect to solve their problems. Recap of the factors in English. Workshop session on body language: hands, facial expressions, eye contact, posture and movement, plus practical remedies for stage fright. Third session of his Friday Sermon Workshop, recorded during the December 2020 lockdown. He restates the 7/38/55 rule: content captures only seven percent of attention, voice about a third and body language the majority, which is why deep scholars go unheard while clowns draw crowds. He then works through four parts of body language. Hands must move, but every gesture should match the meaning and emotion of the words; sudden movements, repeated tics, synchronized robotic motion and finger pointing all break the connection. The face must be lit and unobstructed, and a speaker should smile at least once so people know he is human. Eye contact should last three to four seconds per person and be spontaneous, because looking is how a speaker reads and adjusts to his audience. For posture: stand, face people, never turn your back or side, move in small steps rather than pacing, and do not clutch your own hand. He notes that Jumuah strips away most of these tools, which is why it is the hardest form of speaking. He closes with remedies for stage fright: hold on to something, look just above the last head, use a personal pre-talk routine of dhikr, deep breath and smile, do not cram beforehand, and practise aloud, even to walls or to your own family at home. Hajj, and Mina in particular, teaches Muslims to take agency and make decisions instead of adopting a victim mentality. He opens by listing a heavy stretch of news: the Nakba anniversary, the coming June 6th anniversary, Muslims killed in San Diego, Bill C-9 and the intercepted flotilla. He grounds this in 2:196, which right after commanding Hajj tells the pilgrim who is blocked by an enemy to slaughter, stay in ihram until Eid and come back next year, in other words to do what is still possible rather than go home and cry. He then reads Mina as a place of decision through three storylines: Adam and Hawwa stopped sulking and resolved to earn Jannah back; Ibrahim and Ismail had every excuse for self-pity yet submitted; and the Prophet, humiliated at Taif, banned from Makkah and without a plan, refused the angel's offer to crush his tormentors and hoped for their children instead. Everyone has values, even the worst people, but being ethical means ranking them correctly. A man who cheats to provide for his family has values but no ethics. The Quran shows this ranking: parents are obeyed second only to Allah, but never into shirk, and one must testify truthfully even against parents. Fiqh rulings change with every new fatwa, yet the core values are not disputed; people simply take from Islam what fits their assumptions and justify their choices. The Prophet was sent to perfect noble character, making the order of values clear so that no one could justify harm or oppression through a value. Tempters want a principled person to slip just once, which is why Quraysh, finding no ethical fault in the Prophet, could only call him mad. He urges parents to teach children ethics, not just ritual, and closes with an image of the Prophet's carefully ordered stack of values dropped and restacked wrongly somewhere in history. Al-Razzaq, the Provider

Al-Razzaq: everything you have is provision decreed for you, tied in the Quran to need, gratitude, certainty and giving; starvation comes from withheld shares. He distinguishes Al-Razzaq, the One who provides continuously to all without exception, from the less intensive Ar-Raziq, and defines rizq as anything usable. Rizq becomes a blessing (ni'mah) only when you recognize it as one, so the difference is in your perspective, and everything from your skin colour to your community is rizq. Every creature's provision is upon Allah; Ibrahim's prayer for Mecca was corrected to include disbelievers, and a story has Ibrahim rebuked for evicting a disbelieving guest whom Allah had fed for seventy years. A practical fiqh walk-through of Hajj: the four pillars, the obligatory acts and their expiation, the sunnahs, ihram rules and the sites. This class is the technical half of a two-part Hajj series. The obligatory acts (ihram from the miqat, Muzdalifah, stoning, the farewell tawaf, shaving or cutting the hair, the nights at Mina, staying at Arafah until sunset) do not void Hajj if missed, but require a sacrificial animal, and several missed obligations still cost a single animal per person. He chooses the safest combination of opinions, following the modern Saudi Hajj council, and urges flexibility given three million pilgrims: make the intention for raml, the two rakat behind Maqam Ibrahim or touching the Black Stone rather than endangering anyone. Standing in silence under a near sun, sweating by one's deeds, while seven kinds of people are called into the shade of Allah's Throne. The sun is brought close and people sweat according to their deeds, from the ankles to the mouth, while angels call certain people into a shaded area. He walks through the seven whom Allah shades under His Throne: the just leader at any level, from head of state to father, with every betrayal carried as a banner and the failed public leader the worst traitor; the youth raised in worship; the one whose heart is attached to the masjid; two who love each other only for Allah; the one who refuses a powerful, beautiful seducer out of fear of Allah; the one who gives so secretly his left hand does not know; and the one who remembers Allah in spiritual solitude until his eyes fill with tears. How Quraysh slandered, mocked and harassed the Prophet in the middle Makkan years, and how the Quran, especially Surah al-Kawthar, taught him to respond. When ideas go bankrupt, he argues, people move to mockery and then violence. The Prophet's restraint was a conscious choice, not weakness, shown when he walked into a circle of mocking nobles and warned them. Umm Jamil's garbage and her attempt to strike him with rocks show Allah protecting him from severe humiliation by simply controlling perception. His answer to the Mudhammam poems shows him always finding something to praise. He closes with Surah al-Kawthar as a manual for being mocked: you have nothing to prove, keep praying and keep giving, and harm returns to the one who sends it. Az-Zukhruf warns against materialist logic that judges God, prophets and people, especially women, by wealth and glitter. Delivered partly in English and partly in Arabic, this summary places Az-Zukhruf among the Hawamim, which give advice and warnings for those calling to Allah. Its warning is against the logic of zukhruf, glittering ornament: a materialist mindset that values only what shines and can be measured. Extravagance as a lifestyle does not exempt anyone from the reminder. Materialism makes faith in an unseen God hard, so the surah teaches a prayer when mounting a ship or animal, a reminder that creation has a non-material side. The same logic made pre-Islamic Arabs despise daughters, whose material return seemed lower. He argues that today's consumer culture still values women by appearance, and that the appearance of freedom in this country is false. Hijab, with men's lowered gaze, is meant to make society judge a woman by her character and knowledge. Allah would have given disbelievers silver roofs were it not for people all turning to disbelief. He urges holding fast to revelation and sound reason, which Islam never separates. Al-Hadid closes the cluster by asking not for a choice but for a balance between the spiritual and the material. Al-Hadid is the last surah of the cluster from Qaf, and unlike the others it does not ask us to choose one side over another. The opening verses describe Allah as the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, and say He is with us wherever we are, by His knowledge and attributes rather than physically. The command to believe and to spend from what you hold in trust pairs a spiritual act with a material one. Two men giving the same 200 dinars before and after the conquest of Makkah are not equal, because the earlier one gave in poverty and fear. On the Day of Judgment the believers' light reflects what settled in their hearts, while the hypocrites, who were with them in body but not in spirit, are shut out behind a wall. He calls the verse saying Allah revives the earth after its death the most hopeful in the Quran, since He can revive a dead heart too. Worldly play, adornment and rivalry are not forbidden, but absorption in them hardens hearts. The surah ends with iron and the balance, and rejects monasticism, because neglecting either body or soul breaks the balance. Ramadan 2023, Night 10: Quranic Reflections (At-Tawbah)

At-Tawbah on the ummah's relationships: scholars neither idolised nor dismissed, the cave and sadness, Allah's pleasure, Ibn Ubayy's funeral, honest repentance, and the sale to Allah. Marking a third of Ramadan as a checkpoint, he introduces at-Tawbah as the surah defining the ummah's relationships, which he considers vital for Muslims in Canada. The first is with scholars: earlier communities raised their clergy to near-divine status, who then exploited people's wealth. Muslims swing between treating scholars as infallible and dismissing the whole structure of knowledge; scholars are human and their work must be tested by evidence, and sacred knowledge must never be sold, as his own Quran teacher showed by refusing a gift. In the cave during the hijrah, after every precaution, the Prophet told Abu Bakr not to grieve: fear is natural, but sadness at an unfinished mission is avoided by having done everything possible. Allah's pleasure is greater than all of Paradise, as the Prophet's prayer at Ta'if shows. The Prophet prayed over Abdullah ibn Ubayy out of compassion before the ruling forbade it, showing love behind the law. Those who admit their sins without excuses are the model for repentance, and Allah's purchase of believers' lives and wealth for Paradise shows how highly He values each person, as the Ansar understood at their pledge. A third of the month is done: evaluate what you hoped to achieve and how far you still need to go. Ramadan in thirds: mercy, forgiveness, freedom. The report dividing Ramadan into thirds has weak authenticity, but scholars long accepted the idea, so tonight is the last night of mercy. At-Tawbah: the ummah's relationships. The only surah without the basmalah because of its stern opening; it defines relations with every group inside and outside the ummah, which matters greatly for Muslims in Canada. A healthy relationship with scholars. Other communities placed clergy between human and divine; in Islam scholars and preachers are people held to the same standard, and excess power corrupts them and the deen. Clergy who devour people's wealth. Many rabbis and monks misused people's money; the hoarded gold will be heated and pressed on their foreheads, sides and backs. Two extremes: infallible scholars or none at all. The verse is for us: some Muslims treat scholars' words as sacred and beyond critique, others reject the whole structure of Islamic knowledge; both are unacceptable. Scholars are human: weigh their work by evidence. Their intellectual output must be examined by evidence and reason without diminishing their status, and knowledge must never become a commodity. The teacher who refused a gift. When his father offered money after he completed his Quran recitation, the sheikh was deeply offended and nearly withdrew the ijazah. Sacred knowledge has no price. No sum could compensate for the Quran and Sunnah; both learner and teacher must honour it, because a scholar who degrades himself degrades the knowledge he carries. Do not grieve, Allah is with us. Driven from his home, the Prophet in the cave told his companion not to grieve; Allah sent tranquility and unseen soldiers. Every precaution for the hijrah. He slept outside for a month to normalise it, left at noon, hid three nights in a cave in the opposite direction, had a shepherd cover their tracks and walked without camels. The pursuers at the mouth of the cave. Despite everything they reached the exact cave; Abu Bakr said if one looked down at his feet he would see them. Not fear but sadness. Fear was natural and not forbidden; Abu Bakr's grief was that the mission might end before Medina, and the Prophet reminded him they had done all they could. They simply did not look. No one glanced at the small opening, perhaps Allah's unseen soldiers working in their minds; the pursuers learned only later how close they had been. Courage, and no regrets at the end. The scene teaches bravery and that what we must avoid at life's end is sadness over not having given our lives to Allah. Allah's good pleasure is greater. Amid gardens and every pleasure, the most valuable thing in Paradise is knowing Allah is fully pleased with you. Ta'if: as long as You are not displeased with me. Stoned and stranded, bleeding, the Prophet prayed that he could bear anything provided it was not a sign of Allah's anger; a true Muslim keeps asking whether he pleases Allah. Never displeased with you again. In Paradise Allah declares lasting pleasure with its people, which comforts them more than what no eye has seen. Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the worst of enemies. Claiming Islam, he spread rumours about the Prophet's wife, sabotaged him at Uhud and insulted the companions, while his son was a great companion. The son's request and the funeral prayer. When the tearful son asked, the Prophet could not refuse and prayed over him while Umar protested; the Prophet knew who the hypocrites were, whereas we can only guess. In death the rivalries end. Death shows there is no real winning or losing; understanding it makes you pity even the worst person, now utterly powerless. Revealed afterwards, by design. The prohibition came after the prayer so we would see that the Prophet's attitude was compassion and love, with rulings still to be followed. The verse scholars claimed for themselves. Over a hundred scholars said this verse described them best: those in the middle who admit their sins openly, mixing good and bad deeds. Come clean, with no excuses.
